title: Newton's first and second laws
lede: Force does not cause motion, it causes change in motion, and the bigger the mass, the weaker the change.

cards.heading: Inertia and the first law
cards.body: An object with no net force on it keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed, or stays at rest. Motion at constant velocity needs no explanation; only changes in velocity do. Mass is the measure of inertia, the resistance to having your velocity changed.

cards.heading: The second law
cards.body: Net force equals mass times acceleration, and both force and acceleration are vectors pointing the same way. The forces must be added as vectors before multiplying by mass, and the unit is the newton: 1 N = 1 kg times m/s^2. Note the net force is what matters, not any individual force.

cards.heading: Worked example
cards.body: A 1200 kg car accelerates from rest to 24 m/s in 8.0 s. The acceleration is (24 - 0)/8.0 = 3.0 m/s^2, so the net force is 1200 times 3.0 = 3600 N. That is the net force, not the engine force: friction and drag push backward, and the engine must supply more than 3600 N to win that tug-of-war.

flashcards.meaning: Net force equals mass times acceleration
flashcards.explain: Add every force on the object as a vector first, then divide by mass to get acceleration. The acceleration always points along the net force, never necessarily along the object's velocity.

flashcards.meaning: Equilibrium: zero net force means zero acceleration
flashcards.explain: This is the workhorse of statics and constant-velocity motion. Zero net force does not mean zero motion, it means constant velocity, including the special case of remaining at rest.
One newton is the force that accelerates one kilogram at one meter per second squared. It comes straight from the second law's units, which is handy for catching unit errors in exam problems.

mcq.prompt: A 2.5 kg object is pushed by a 3.0 N force east and a 4.0 N force north at the same time. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?
mcq.rightExplain: The forces are perpendicular, so the net force is sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = 5.0 N, and a = F/m = 5.0/2.5 = 2.0 m/s^2.
mcq.wrongExplain: 2.8 m/s^2 adds the force magnitudes directly, 3 + 4 = 7 N, which overcounts because the forces are at right angles. 1.4 m/s^2 divides by mass after averaging the forces instead of combining them as vectors, and 0.5 m/s^2 would need a net force of only 1.25 N, less than either applied force.

title: Free-body diagrams
lede: Draw only the forces acting on the object itself, and most mechanics problems solve themselves.

cards.heading: How to draw one
cards.body: Shrink the object to a dot and draw one arrow for each external force acting on it, with tails starting at the dot and lengths reflecting relative sizes. Include only forces on the object, never forces the object exerts on other things, and never add a separate arrow for ma, which is the result of the forces, not one of them.

cards.heading: Normal force and tension
cards.body: The normal force is a surface pushing perpendicular to itself, and it adjusts itself to whatever makes the perpendicular motion come out right, so it is not always equal to mg. In an elevator accelerating up at 2 m/s^2, the floor must push with m(g + 2). Tension in a rope pulls along the rope toward both ends, and a rope around an ideal pulley has the same tension throughout.

cards.heading: Inclines and components
cards.body: On a slope, tilt your axes so x runs along the incline and y is perpendicular to it. The weight then decomposes into mg sin(theta) down the slope and mg cos(theta) into the surface. For a 10 kg block on a 30 degree incline, those components are 98 sin(30) = 49 N along the slope and 98 cos(30) = 84.9 N into the surface, which is what sets the normal force on a frictionless incline.

flashcards.meaning: Normal force in an upward-accelerating elevator
flashcards.explain: Newton's second law in the vertical direction: the floor's push must both support the weight and supply the upward acceleration. The scale reads this normal force, which is why you feel heavier on launch.

flashcards.meaning: Weight components along and into an incline
flashcards.explain: Rotating axes so one axis lies along the slope turns a two-dimensional problem into two one-dimensional ones. The sine component drives sliding; the cosine component sets the normal force and therefore friction.

flashcards.meaning: Ideal rope pulls equally on both attached objects
flashcards.explain: An ideal massless rope over an ideal pulley transmits the same tension everywhere. Each attached object feels that tension pulling toward the rope, so one T value links both halves of a pulley problem.

mcq.prompt: A 50 kg person stands in an elevator accelerating upward at 2.0 m/s^2. What does the scale read? Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.
mcq.rightExplain: Newton's second law gives N - mg = ma, so N = m(g + a) = 50(9.8 + 2.0) = 590 N.
mcq.wrongExplain: 490 N is the plain weight, which is the reading only when the elevator is at rest or at constant speed, and 390 N uses a sign error, computing m(g - a) as if the elevator accelerated downward. 980 N doubles the weight, as if the acceleration equaled g.

title: Static and kinetic friction
lede: Friction has two regimes, and the static one has a maximum rather than a fixed value.

cards.heading: Static vs kinetic
cards.body: Static friction acts when surfaces do not slide; it adjusts itself to exactly cancel the applied push, up to a maximum of mu_s N. Once sliding starts, kinetic friction takes over with a fixed magnitude mu_k N opposing the sliding direction. Because mu_s exceeds mu_k, it takes more force to start a slide than to keep one going, which is why heavy boxes lurch.

cards.heading: The coefficient and N
cards.body: The coefficient of friction is dimensionless and depends only on the pair of surfaces, not on the size of the forces. The friction formula uses the normal force, not the weight, so on an incline friction is mu times mg cos(theta), weaker than on level ground. On a level surface at rest, N equals mg.

cards.heading: Worked example
cards.body: A 5.0 kg block slides down a 37 degree incline with mu_k = 0.25, using sin(37) = 0.60 and cos(37) = 0.80. Gravity pulls along the slope with 49(0.60) = 29.4 N. The normal force is 49(0.80) = 39.2 N, so kinetic friction is 0.25 times 39.2 = 9.8 N up the slope. The net 19.6 N along the slope gives a = 19.6/5.0 = 3.92 m/s^2 down the incline.

flashcards.meaning: Static friction can be anything up to a maximum
flashcards.explain: Static friction is reactive, matching the applied force push for push until its ceiling. Only at the moment sliding impends does it reach its maximum value mu_s times N.

flashcards.meaning: Kinetic friction is fixed while sliding
flashcards.explain: Once surfaces slide, friction has one magnitude regardless of applied force, opposing the motion. The relevant N is the perpendicular squeeze between the surfaces, which equals the weight only on level ground.

flashcards.meaning: It takes more force to start sliding than to maintain it
flashcards.explain: The static ceiling sits above the kinetic value for the same surfaces. This gap explains the stick-slip lurch of a heavy crate or the squeal of a chalk stick skipping down a board.

mcq.prompt: A 20 kg crate sits on a level floor with mu_s = 0.40 and mu_k = 0.30. What horizontal force keeps it sliding at constant speed?
mcq.rightExplain: Once sliding, friction is kinetic: f_k = 0.30(20)(9.8) = 58.8 N, and constant speed means the push must exactly balance it, about 59 N.
mcq.wrongExplain: 78 N is the static maximum, mu_s N = 0.40(196), which is the force to start the crate moving, not to keep it going. 196 N is the normal force with the coefficient forgotten, and 20 N merely restates the mass in newtons by coincidence of numbers.

title: Centripetal force in circles
lede: Circular motion needs a real force pointed at the center, and identifying which force plays that role is the whole problem.

cards.heading: Centripetal acceleration
cards.body: An object in uniform circular motion is accelerating even at constant speed, because the direction of the velocity vector keeps changing. The acceleration points toward the center with magnitude v^2/r, growing with speed and shrinking with radius. Doubling the speed quadruples the required force.

cards.heading: What provides it
cards.body: There is no new kind of force called centripetal force; the word names a role. Tension pulls a swung ball toward your hand, gravity keeps satellites in orbit, and friction points toward the center for a car on a flat curve. Newton's second law applied radially reads: the sum of real forces toward the center equals m v^2/r.

cards.heading: Worked example
cards.body: A 0.50 kg ball is swung in a horizontal circle on a 1.5 m string at 6.0 m/s. The centripetal acceleration is 36/1.5 = 24 m/s^2, so the string tension must be 0.50 times 24 = 12 N. If the string can only hold 10 N, the ball cannot be swung that fast: at the breaking tension the maximum speed is sqrt(10(1.5)/0.50) = sqrt(30) = 5.5 m/s.

flashcards.explain: The direction-changing acceleration of uniform circular motion. It is perpendicular to the velocity, so it turns the motion without changing the speed.

flashcards.meaning: Radial Newton's second law for circular motion
flashcards.explain: Write the second law along the radius, inward positive, with whatever real forces act: tension, gravity, friction, or a combination. This single equation is the entire dynamics of a circle problem.

flashcards.meaning: Maximum cornering speed on a flat curve
flashcards.explain: Friction is the only force available to turn the car on a flat road, so mu N = mu mg must supply m v^2/r. Above this speed, friction cannot bend the path fast enough and the car skids outward.

mcq.prompt: A car takes a flat curve of radius 50 m at 20 m/s. What minimum coefficient of static friction keeps it on the road? Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.
mcq.rightExplain: Friction must supply the centripetal force: mu mg = mv^2/r, so mu = v^2/(gr) = 400/(9.8)(50) = 0.82.
mcq.wrongExplain: 0.20 effectively halves the ratio by mixing in an extra factor, and 1.2 would have friction supply about 11.8 m/s^2 of turning when the curve demands only 8.0 m/s^2.
